questions.explanation: 「山」 means mountain: やま (yama). It began as a picture of three peaks.
「川」 means river: かわ (kawa). Its three lines run down like flowing water, where 「三」 (three) has three lines across.
「木」 means tree: き (ki). 「本」 (book) is the same tree with a short line added near the roots.
「日」 means sun: ひ (hi), and it also means day. 「目」 (eye) has two lines inside the box, and 「日」 has one.
「目」 means eye: め (me). It has two lines inside its tall box, where 「日」 (sun) has one.
「口」 means mouth: くち (kuchi). It is an empty square, where 「田」 (rice field) is divided into four.
「耳」 means ear: みみ (mimi). 「目」 (eye) is similar but has no strokes sticking out at the bottom and side.
「火」 means fire: ひ (hi). It is also the 火 in 火よう日, Tuesday.
「水」 means water: みず (mizu). It is also the 水 in 水よう日, Wednesday.
「金」 means gold: きん (kin) in 金よう日, Friday, and かね (kane) when it means money. Silver has a kanji of its own.
「土」 means soil: つち (tsuchi), and ど (do) in 土よう日, Saturday. 「上」 (up) has its short stroke on the right, not across.
「田」 means rice field: た (ta). It is a field divided into four plots. 「口」 (mouth) is the same square with nothing inside.
「人」 means person: ひと (hito). Its two strokes meet at the top, like a person standing; in 「八」 (eight) they do not touch.
「大」 means big: the first kanji of 大きい (ookii). It is 「人」 (person) with arms spread wide.
「中」 means inside: なか (naka), inside or middle, as in かばんの中 (kaban no naka, inside the bag). Its line goes straight through the middle of the box.
「男」 means man: おとこ (otoko). It has 「田」 (rice field) on top, but the whole kanji means man.
「友」 means friend: とも (tomo), as in 友だち (tomodachi).
「父」 means father: ちち (chichi). The top two strokes look like 「八」 (eight), but the cross underneath makes it father.
「今」 means now: いま (ima), as in 今何時ですか (ima nanji desu ka, what time is it now).
「何」 means what: なに or なん (nani, nan), as in 何時 (nanji, what time).
「年」 means year: ねん (nen) after a number, as in 一年生 (ichinensei, a first-year student).
「半」 means half: はん (han). After a time it means half past: 二時半 (niji han) is 2:30.
「月」 means moon. It is つき (tsuki) on its own, げつ (getsu) in 月よう日 and がつ (gatsu) in the months. 「日」 is sun.
「女」 means woman. It is おんな (onna), as in 女の子 (onna no ko, girl). 「母」 is mother.
「子」 means child. It is こ (ko), as in 女の子 and 男の子. 「手」 (hand) has extra strokes across.
「母」 means mother. It is はは (haha), and お母さん (okaasan) when you talk about someone else's mother.
「小」 means small. It is the first kanji of 小さい (chiisai). 「川」 is river and 「大」 is big.
「上」 means above. It is うえ (ue), and its short stroke points up. 「下」 (below) points down.
「手」 means hand. It is て (te). 「千」 (thousand) has only one stroke across.
「千」 means thousand. It is せん (sen). 「十」 is ten and 「百」 is a hundred.
「日本」 is にほん (nihon), Japan. Here 日 is read に, although on its own it is ひ (hi), and in 日よう日 it is にち (nichi).
人 after a country is じん (jin): にほんじん (nihonjin), a Japanese person, like オーストラリアじん. It is にん (nin) after a number, as in 三人.
「先生」 is せんせい (sensei), teacher. 先 means ahead and 生 means born: someone born before you.
学 on its own is がく (gaku), but before こう its く becomes a small っ: がっこう (gakkou), school.
「大きい」 is おおきい (ookii), big. Its long o is written with お, not う, which is why おうきい is a common spelling mistake.
「小さい」 is ちいさい (chiisai), small, with a long i. 小 is read ちい here and the hiragana さい follows it.
「見ます」 is みます (mimasu), to see or watch. 見 is read み, and ます is the ending.

questions.stem: How do you read 「行きます」?
questions.explanation: 「行きます」 is いきます (ikimasu), to go. 行 is read い and the hiragana きます follows it.
「来ます」 is きます (kimasu), to come. The same kanji is read く in くる and こ in こない, so it is a good example of one kanji with several readings.

questions.stem: How do you read 「食べます」?
questions.explanation: 「食べます」 is たべます (tabemasu), to eat. 食 is read た and べます is written in hiragana after it.

questions.stem: How do you read 「飲みます」?
questions.explanation: 「飲みます」 is のみます (nomimasu), to drink. 飲 is read の and みます follows it.
One person is ひとり (hitori), not いち plus a counter. ふたり (futari) is two people, and from three on it uses にん: さんにん (sannin), よにん (yonin).
Two people is ふたり (futari). Like ひとり, it is a special reading that has to be learned on its own.
Four people is よにん (yonin): 四 is よ here, not よん. し is avoided because it sounds like the word for death.

questions.stem: In 「かぞくは何人ですか。」, how is 「何人」 read?
questions.explanation: Asking how many people is なんにん (nannin): 何 becomes なん before a counter, and 人 is にん when counting people.

questions.stem: In 「今何時ですか。」, how is 「何時」 read?
questions.explanation: 「何時」 is なんじ (nanji), what time. 何 becomes なん before the counter 時, so the question is いまなんじですか (ima nanji desu ka).
Four o'clock is よじ (yoji). 四 is usually よん, but with 時 it shortens to よ, and よんじ is a very common mistake.
Nine o'clock is くじ (kuji). 九 is usually きゅう, but with 時 it is always く.
After 三, 百 changes from ひゃく to びゃく: さんびゃくえん (sanbyaku en), 300 yen. The p sound belongs to 六百 and 八百 instead.
六 shortens to ろっ and 百 becomes ぴゃく: ろっぴゃくえん (roppyaku en), 600 yen.
八 shortens to はっ and 百 becomes ぴゃく: はっぴゃくえん (happyaku en), 800 yen.
After 三, 千 changes from せん to ぜん: さんぜんえん (sanzen en), 3,000 yen. The other thousands keep せん; only 八 changes too, giving はっせん.

questions.stem: How do you read 「一分」, one minute?
questions.explanation: 一 shortens to いっ and 分 becomes ぷん: いっぷん (ippun). 五分 (gofun) keeps ふん, so the sound depends on the number before it.

questions.stem: In 「日よう日」, how is each 日 read?
questions.explanation: Sunday is にちようび (nichiyoubi): the first 日 is にち and the second is び, a softened ひ. The middle part is in hiragana because its kanji comes later.

questions.stem: How do you read 「月よう日」?
questions.explanation: Monday is げつようび (getsuyoubi). 月 is げつ here, がつ in the months, as in 一月 (ichigatsu), and つき when it means the moon.

questions.stem: How do you read 「金よう日」?
questions.explanation: Friday is きんようび (kin'youbi). 金 is きん here, but かね when it means money.

questions.stem: How do you read 「土よう日」?
questions.explanation: Saturday is どようび (doyoubi). 土 is ど here, but つち when it means soil.

questions.stem: How do you read 「お父さん」?
questions.explanation: 「お父さん」 is おとうさん (otousan), someone else's father. Your own father is 父, read ちち (chichi), which is why おちちさん is a tempting mix of the two.

questions.stem: In 「母は先生です。」, how is 「母」 read?
questions.explanation: Talking about your own mother, 母 is はは (haha): はははせんせいです (haha wa sensei desu), my mother is a teacher. かあ is its reading inside お母さん (okaasan), not on its own.
「友だち」 is ともだち (tomodachi), friend. 友 is read とも and だち is written in hiragana.

questions.stem: In 「山に行きます。」, how is 「山」 read?
questions.explanation: 「山」 is やま (yama), mountain: やまにいきます (yama ni ikimasu), I go to the mountains. かわ (kawa) is 川, river.

questions.stem: In 「つくえの上」, how is 「上」 read?
questions.explanation: つくえのうえ (tsukue no ue) is on top of the desk. 下 (した) is under and 中 (なか) is inside; じょう is a reading of 上 used in other words.

questions.stem: In 「かばんの中」, how is 「中」 read?
questions.explanation: かばんのなか (kaban no naka) is inside the bag. ちゅう is a reading of 中 used in longer words, not after の.
五 (five) before 百 (hundred) multiplies: 五百 is 500, ごひゃくえん (gohyaku en). 5,000 yen would be 五千円.
七時 is seven o'clock and 半 is half: しちじはん (shichiji han), half past seven.
A number before 十 multiplies it and a number after adds: 五十 is 50, and 六 more makes 56, ごじゅうろく (gojuuroku).

questions.stem: Which day of the week is 「水よう日」?
questions.explanation: 水 (water) gives すいようび (suiyoubi), Wednesday. The week runs 日 月 火 水 木 金 土, Sunday to Saturday.

questions.stem: Which day of the week is 「火よう日」?
questions.explanation: 火 (fire) gives かようび (kayoubi), Tuesday. 水よう日 is Wednesday and 木よう日 is Thursday.

questions.stem: Which kanji began as a picture of three mountain peaks?
questions.explanation: 「山」 (やま, yama) still shows its three peaks, the middle one tallest. Several of the first kanji began as pictures like this.

questions.stem: Which kanji began as a picture of a river?
questions.explanation: 「川」 (かわ, kawa) shows water running between banks. 「三」 (three) has its three lines lying across instead.

questions.stem: Which kanji began as a picture of a tree, with branches above and roots below?
questions.explanation: 「木」 (き, ki) is a trunk with branches and roots. 「大」 (big) is a person with arms spread wide.

questions.stem: Which kanji began as a picture of the sun?
questions.explanation: 「日」 (ひ, hi) began as a circle with a mark in the middle and was squared off over time. It means both sun and day.

questions.stem: Which kanji began as a picture of an eye, later stood on end?
questions.explanation: 「目」 (め, me) was first drawn as an eye lying sideways, then turned upright to fit a column of writing. 「日」, with one line inside, is the sun.

questions.stem: Which kanji began as a picture of an open mouth?
questions.explanation: 「口」 (くち, kuchi) is the shape of an open mouth. 「田」 is a rice field divided into plots.

questions.stem: What does a single kanji carry?
options: a meaning only, with no reading
a sound only, like a letter
questions.explanation: Each kanji stands for a meaning and has at least one reading: 「山」 means mountain and is read やま (yama). Kana stand for sounds alone.

questions.stem: Why can 日 be read に, にち, ひ and び?
options: a kanji can have several readings, depending on the word
each reading belongs to a different kanji that looks the same
only one reading is correct and the others are mistakes
the reading depends on which region the speaker is from
questions.explanation: Many kanji have several readings, and the word decides which one: 日本 (にほん), 日よう日 (にちようび), and 日 on its own (ひ). Learning the kanji inside common words is the reliable way to learn its readings.

questions.stem: In 「大きい」, what is the hiragana 「きい」 after 大 called?
questions.explanation: Okurigana are the hiragana that follow a kanji to complete the word, often its ending. Furigana are the small kana printed above a kanji to show its reading.

questions.stem: In 「見ます」, what is the hiragana 「ます」?
options: okurigana, the ending that follows the kanji
furigana showing how the kanji is read
a separate word meaning to see or look
a particle that marks the object
questions.explanation: 見 carries the meaning see and ます is the polite verb ending, written in hiragana after the kanji as okurigana. The verb changes by changing the okurigana: 見ません (mimasen), 見ました (mimashita).

questions.stem: In 「食べます」, which part does the kanji 食 write?
questions.explanation: 食 is read た, and everything after it, べます, is okurigana. That is why the word is 食べます, not 食ます.

options: showing how a kanji is read
questions.explanation: Furigana are small kana, usually hiragana, printed with a kanji so a reader can say it. Children's books and texts for learners use them on kanji the reader may not know yet.

questions.stem: In horizontal writing, where are furigana usually printed?
options: to the left of the kanji
questions.explanation: In horizontal text furigana sit above the kanji. In vertical text they go to the right of it.

questions.stem: Where did kanji originally come from?
questions.explanation: Kanji are Chinese characters, which reached Japan many centuries ago. Hiragana and katakana were later made from them to write Japanese sounds.

questions.stem: Which basic stroke-order rule does 「三」 follow?
questions.explanation: The three lines of 「三」 are written from the top down. Top to bottom and left to right are the two rules nearly every kanji follows.

questions.stem: Which basic stroke-order rule does 「川」 follow?
questions.explanation: The three strokes of 「川」 are written from the left, so the curved left-hand stroke comes first and the long right-hand stroke last.

questions.stem: In 「十」, which stroke is written first?
options: both are written as one stroke
questions.explanation: When a horizontal and a vertical stroke cross, the horizontal usually comes first, as in 「十」 and 「千」.

questions.stem: In 「中」, which stroke is written last?
options: the left side of the box
questions.explanation: A stroke that runs right through a kanji is usually written last, so the box of 「中」 is finished before the central line goes through it.

questions.stem: In 「口」, when is the bottom line written?
questions.explanation: 「口」 has three strokes: the left side, then the top and right side in one stroke, then the bottom line to close the box. The same rule closes 「日」 and 「目」.
